title: How to Add a Second Product Category on Gooten Without Rebuilding Fulfillment
excerpt: A practical sequence for expanding a print-on-demand catalog into a new category on Gooten: prove demand, map the operational differences, then scale without resetting your fulfillment rules.
body: Adding a second product category grows average order value quickly, and breaks working fulfillment even faster. Your catalog already spans apparel, wall art, drinkware and home goods, so it is tempting to switch one on the week a design starts selling. Each category carries its own production time, packaging rules and carrier options, and those differences leak into the promises you already make at checkout. A deliberate sequence costs a few weeks and saves a season of refund tickets.

Start with demand, not with the catalog. Prove that existing buyers want the new category before you upload a single mockup, using a waitlist on the page, a short pre-order window, or a poll sent to last quarter's buyers. Pick the numeric bar in advance, whether that is twenty committed orders or two hundred clicks from your email list in a week. Without a bar, you cannot tell a category that deserves investment from one that only looked good in planning.

Once the bar is met, map the operational differences before touching a listing. Put production time, ship-to regions, dimensional weight behavior and damage claim handling for the new category side by side with the same fields for your current one. That sheet tells you whether the shipping prices shown at checkout still hold, and which policies need rewriting, because a fragile item and a folded tee should not share the same returns copy.

Check routing and shipping profiles next. Every variant you sell has to resolve to a facility that can produce it and a shipping method you are willing to defend publicly. Unmapped variants are the expensive failure mode here, because they either stall in a queue or silently fall back to the slowest available route. The Gooten page at /tool/gooten keeps current notes on categories, production behavior and constraints, and the DTCwise Fulfillment & Shipping category at /category/fulfillment covers the rest of the stack you touch during the move.

Now set the customer-facing promises. Update the shipping page with a production handling time that reflects the slower of your two categories, or split the promise by product type if your theme supports it. Decide who pays for a replacement when an item arrives damaged, and how quickly a claim must be filed. Fold those answers into the FAQ you already publish instead of creating a second one, so support has a single source of truth during the transition.

Run a pilot of thirty to fifty real orders before you scale, and compare four numbers against your existing baseline: production time variance, damage rate per hundred orders, support tickets per hundred orders, and contribution margin after shipping and refunds. Variance matters more than the average. A category that averages four days but occasionally takes eleven generates complaints even while the mean looks healthy on a dashboard.

Widen the catalog only when those numbers sit inside the thresholds you set, and leave the working category untouched while you do it. Keep new products in their own collection for the first month so tracking stays clean, then promote winners into evergreen navigation. Revisit the same mapping sheet every time you expand, because that work gets faster on each round.
